chunks: Prayer is broken by flatulence when it comes out from the one praying, or by anything else that breaks the wudu, or by remembering that one is not in a state of wudu, or by experiencing an injury, or a severe throbbing pain that one is unable to endure, or a nosebleed in which a great deal of blood flows from the nose, or by turning around until one sees what is behind oneself.
The prayer of a Muslim is not broken by anything passing before him, whether a dog, a woman, a donkey, or anything else.

key_terms.الريح: Flatulence/wind — here a euphemism for passing wind during prayer, which breaks wudu and thus invalidates prayer
key_terms.الضربان: Throbbing pain — severe enough to prevent continuity of prayer
key_terms.رعف: Epistaxis/nosebleed — ruled here to be a prayer-breaker when blood is copious
key_terms.ينقض الوضوء: That which nullifies ritual purity (wudu) — the standard categories in fiqh

ai.seo_question: What are the things that invalidate (break) prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Amali of Sheikh al-Saduq enumerates the conditions that break (invalidate) prayer versus those popularly believed to break prayer but actually do not. The ruling clarifies that internal bodily occurrences — such as passing wind, loss of ritual purity, serious pain, or a nosebleed — are genuine invalidators, while external creatures or persons passing before the worshipper do not interrupt prayer. This ruling counters a widespread belief prevalent in some hadith traditions that a dog, woman, or donkey passing before a worshipper breaks their prayer.
